title: Meadowlane inference migration alignment

Key concerns: eval parity with vLLM/TGI stacks, latency/cost tradeoffs, VPC/on‑prem constraints, KMS encryption, SOC2/ISO. Agreed to run a parity benchmark (10k prompt set) and share security pack. Next SE deep dive to run perf tests against customer's TGI/vLLM baseline.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-05-03 08:00 PDT / 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Caleb (Redwood SE), Lina (Redwood solutions), Jordan (Meadowlane Head of ML), Priya (CTO), Omar (Infra), Dana (SRE)

Summary: quick intro, then deep dive on parity with vLLM/TGI, security, and hosting options.

[00:00] Maya Ortiz: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya with Redwood Inference, and with me is Caleb our SE and Lina who does solutions. How's everyone?

[00:12] Jordan Bell: hey Maya, good thanks, busy quarter but excited. We just wanna see if moving off our current stack makes sense.

[00:20] Priya Rao: hi all, quick context — we're Meadowlane Analytics, product is a clinical insights assistant, currently using mix of OpenAI hosted for safety-critical flows and Azure ML endpoints for some heavy‑duty models via TGI in house. Cost is spiking, latency sometimes flares, and we had a couple OOM incidents during peak.

[00:41] Caleb Turner: thanks. Can you give a bit more on model footprint, token sizes, QPS? Even rough numbers help — seq length, percent long ctx, average tokens per request?

[00:53] Jordan Bell: sure, rough: avg seq ~600 tokens, 6% of calls >2k, peak QPS ~60 across all regions, most traffic US-east, then EU-west. Baseline is a mixture: 50% chat gpt-like flows (we route to OpenAI), 50% heavy gen + reranking on TGI/vLLM stack on Azure infra. 

[01:25] Maya Ortiz: got it. So main drivers are cost predictability, reliability (avoid OOM/GC from vLLM spikes), and eval parity — you want the same output quality across runs?

[01:35] Jordan Bell: exactly, parity is critical. We baked a large eval set (ten thousand prompts) with ground truth scoring. We need to make sure switching runtimes doesn't change the model outputs in ways that break downstream signals.

[01:50] Dana Liu: also security — SOC2 and KMS. We need key custody and audit logs. We want to avoid sending PHI to third party unless encrypted or within VPC.

[02:05] Caleb Turner: totally understood. High level: Redwood supports hosted API for trials, Dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and Private deployments (VPC or on‑prem) for locked down workloads. For eval parity: we typically run an eval parity benchmark where we run your 10k set on Redwood and on your vLLM/TGI baseline and compare logits, tokens, and downstream metric diffs.

[02:30] Priya Rao: do you support TGI models out of the box? A lot of our in‑house is TGI-wrapped Mistral/llama variants.

[02:38] Caleb Turner: two parts — we have model catalog and can host many containerized model artifacts. For TGI/vLLM compatibility we usually test at runtime. In many cases Redwood runtime replicates outputs within noise, but occasionally tokenization or different kernel ordering changes whitespace or rare tokens. We surface those diffs with a delta report.

[02:56] Jordan Bell: okay, those small token diffs are fine as long as downstream metrics don't degrade. Any examples of customers who did a parity run and had regressions?

[03:10] Caleb Turner: yes — one customer ported a reranker and saw a 2.7% drop in NDCG because of tokenizer scoring differences, we identified it was a byte-level decode mismatch and fixed by using the same tokenizer artifact. So the process is: run full eval, produce token‑level diffs, and if needed we pin tokenizer and kernel flags or use a compatible model variant.

[03:36] Maya Ortiz: on hosting modes — if you need quick early validation, hosted API gives fastest time-to-value and we can do a sandbox dedicated pool for consistent perf. If you have compliance needs and want key control, Redwood Private (VPC or on‑prem) is typical. Dedicated sits in middle — reserved pools with VPC peering.

[03:55] Omar Singh: curious on encryption and KMS flow — we use cloud KMS and would need HSM or bring your own KMS for private keys.

[04:05] Lina Park: we integrate with customer KMS providers — you can bring keys (BYOK) for Private deployments; for dedicated we support KMS integration and provide envelope encryption. Audit logs are available and we can forward to your SIEM.

[04:22] Priya Rao: latency numbers? we require p95 < 220ms for conversational flows; for longer generation we accept p95 ~1.2s but must avoid large tail latencies.

[04:34] Caleb Turner: depends on model and batch config. For 8k‑token models with careful batching we often see p95 ~150–200ms for 512 token-ish calls on our Dedicated pools with GPU-optimized kernels. For long sequences latency grows — we can tailor batching and KV cache to keep tail down. Also we do graceful degradation: fallback to smaller quantized variant if serving pool is constrained.

[04:58] Jordan Bell: we hit OOMs in vLLM during peak peaks, which required full restarts. How do you handle memory fragmentation and KV cache eviction?

[05:10] Caleb Turner: our runtime has continuous batching and explicit KV cache management; we support automatic prefix cache persistence to avoid reloads and can evict cold keys. We also pick kernels/quantization levels based on seq-length distribution to avoid fragmentation. If we detect sustained pressure we can route lower-priority requests to a quantized model variant.

[05:32] Dana Liu: any limits on model size? we have Mistral XXL-ish and some 70B variants.

[05:40] Caleb Turner: we host up to very large models depending on deployment type; Dedicated and Private can be sized for 70B+ with partitioned kernels. Hosted catalog may have curated larger models too but for extremely large custom weights Private is recommended.

[05:56] Priya Rao: cost — how predictable is Dedicated vs hosted? our CFO wants line-item predictability for next FY.

[06:05] Maya Ortiz: Dedicated is committed capacity with monthly/annual contracts — predictable. Hosted is pay-as-you-go and cheaper for bursty but less predictable at scale. For many customers we do an initial hosted pilot then move to Dedicated when stable volumes are known.

[06:20] Jordan Bell: great. For parity benchmarking — what's needed from us?

[06:27] Caleb Turner: the eval set, sample traffic distributions (token histograms), and your model artifacts or at least exact repo references for tokenizer. Ideally a container or model repo so we can run exact same weights if you want output parity. Otherwise we compare against your vLLM/TGI endpoint responses.

[06:44] Omar Singh: security pack — we'll need SOC2 Type II, ISO cert, SAML SSO, RBAC, and proof of separation of customer data. Also options for air-gapped deployment if needed.

[06:55] Lina Park: we will send the security pack, plus our runbook for Private deployments. For air-gapped we do a different packaging flow with on‑prem bundle.

[07:05] Jordan Bell: any gotchas when moving from TGI to Redwood runtime? we use some model optimizations in vLLM (kernel patches, patched rotary embeddings) — will that shift outputs?

[07:18] Caleb Turner: sometimes yes — custom kernel patches can affect numerical ordering. We try to keep fidelity by supporting the same tokenization and matching attention mechanisms; if you use patched rotary we replicate flags. The parity run will highlight anything.

[07:34] Priya Rao: what's a realistic timeline for pilot -> dedicated?

[07:39] Maya Ortiz: typical: 1–2 week hosted pilot for functional parity, 2–4 weeks of perf + cost benchmarking, then Dedicated provisioning 2–6 weeks depending on capacity and procurement. Private on‑prem is longer — 6–10 weeks.

[07:53] Dana Liu: procurement and legal — do you have template contracts? We'll need DPAs and specific SLAs on uptime and data deletion.

[08:01] Maya Ortiz: yes we have standard enterprise templates; we'll attach DPAs and SLA terms in the security pack.

[08:08] Jordan Bell: ok let's talk specifics: we'll share the 10k prompt eval and a test TGI endpoint. Can you run Redwood hosted against that?

[08:16] Caleb Turner: yes we can run it against hosted sandbox. Two notes: tokenization must match — please include the tokenizer artifact or exact HF repo and commit. We'll produce a delta report showing token diffs, perplexity differences, and downstream metric diff (your NDCG/Rouge etc).

[08:33] Omar Singh: also we need to measure cost per 1M tokens across setups — include batching overhead and inc autoscale.

[08:40] Maya Ortiz: we'll include cost model estimates in the results, with assumptions on batching, peak windows, and caching hit rates.

[08:48] Jordan Bell: great. Any immediate blockers?

[08:51] Caleb Turner: none. One small fiction — sometimes our automerged; excuse me — autobalancer will route test requests to compatible variants which may slightly change outputs; we'll disable that during parity runs to get deterministic results.

[09:05] Priya Rao: ok good. On the question of RBAC and logs — do you provide token-level audit logs?

[09:12] Lina Park: yes, you can get per-token cost and user-level tracing, and export logs to your SIEM. We also support per-route retention policies.

[09:22] Jordan Bell: fantastic. Let's capture next steps and owners.

[09:26] Maya Ortiz: recap — Meadowlane to share: eval set (10k prompts), tokenizer artifact or model container refs, sample traffic histograms, and a test TGI endpoint. Redwood to: run parity benchmark, share delta report, send security pack and pricing for Dedicated. We'll aim to reconvene after the benchmark.

[09:45] Omar Singh: noted. Any other questions from the team?

[09:47] Dana Liu: none from me.

[09:49] Priya Rao: no. Thanks — appreciate the clarity.

[09:51] Maya Ortiz: thanks everyone — we'll send follow-ups and schedule the SE deep dive for the perf tests.

[09:58] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: medium — occasional word swaps, some product names transcribed as T G I / v L M inconsistently.
